demo.title: Run the search one iteration at a time
demo.caption: An abstract search tree: nodes are dialogue states and the three decomposition strategy names, with no request content. Rewards are illustrative judge scores you can adjust; the UCT values and visit counts are computed live with the paper’s formulas. Step through selection, expansion, simulation and backpropagation.

story.title: Conversation history belongs in the safety test
paragraphs: A model that refuses a harmful request in one turn may still answer its parts across several, because earlier turns change how later ones are read. DAMON (Dialogue-Aware MONte Carlo Tree Search Attack) is a red-teaming method that searches for a sequence of sub-instructions that hides a refused request's intent yet still elicits a harmful response.

The paper names two requirements: query-aware decomposition, because requests need different splits, and strategy-aware refinement, because the plan must change when the victim model refuses part of it.

mechanism.title: Tree search chooses how to decompose each refused turn
paragraphs: Each tree node is an attack state: the answered part of the dialogue, the sub-instructions still refused, an evaluation score, and a visit count. An action is one of three hand-designed decomposition strategies (progressive inquiry, step-by-step questioning, or story-driven imagination), applied by an attack LLM to the first refused sub-instruction.

Each iteration runs the four MCTS stages. Selection descends the tree by UCT (Upper Confidence bounds applied to Trees), adding an exploration bonus for rarely visited children to each child's mean score. Expansion decomposes the selected node with every strategy. Simulation sends the remaining sub-instructions to the victim, a GPT-4o reward model scores the dialogue for harm, and turns before the first new refusal join the stored dialogue. Backpropagation updates mean scores and visit counts up to the root.

Refusal pruning skips states in which every sub-instruction was answered: further splitting rarely restores the original objective once the dialogue has drifted. The attacker needs only black-box access to the victim's outputs and the reward scores.

evidence.title: Adaptive search outperforms fixed-pattern attacks in most settings
paragraphs: Across 15 model–dataset pairs (five victim models on AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, and HarmBench), DAMON has the highest attack success rate in 14; the exception is GPT-4o on HarmBench. A small human check agrees: on 20 HarmBench instances with GPT-4o, three annotators judge 85.0% of DAMON's responses harmful and on-task, versus 75.0% for ActorAttack.

Context matters: replaying DAMON's sub-instructions with no preceding dialogue lowers success substantially, and even random unrelated context raises it above the no-context level. Among defenses, a moderation guardrail barely changes success, perplexity filtering lowers it modestly, and paraphrasing works best, yet average success under paraphrasing is still 71%. The authors hypothesize that a gap between pretraining data and safety-alignment data underlies such failures.

reading_notes: Read main method at conceptual level, Section4 complete, Tables1–4, Figure4 context test, limitations. Page intentionally omits operational attack prompts, search configurations, traces, decompositions and exploit demo. Human sample20, three annotators, majority. Do not claim all baselines outperformed in every cell: ActorAttack84.5 versus DAMON84.0 on GPT4o/HarmBench. No numerical efficiency claims as attempts and walltime are not interchangeable.
